definition: A camera's motion is rigged from three independently-editable pieces rather than one fused position+rotation transform: (1) the PATH's shape — a curve object, edited purely as static geometry with no timing information at all; (2) PROGRESS along that path over time — a single numeric value (a Follow-Path constraint's offset) keyframed to control speed/timing without touching the path's shape; and (3) where the camera LOOKS — a separate target object (constrained to the camera via Track-To) keyframed completely independently of the path or the camera's own position, so the camera can fly along one authored curve while its attention drifts to, holds on, or whips toward targets on an entirely separate timeline.
purpose: Let each of the three concerns that make up a camera move — the geometric shape of the move, the timing/speed of traveling it, and what the shot is actually looking at — be authored and revised independently, so that (for example) slowing the camera down does not require re-shaping the path, and changing what the camera looks at does not require re-timing the move.
visible_effect: The path's curve can be reshaped in edit mode with zero effect on timing; the offset's keyframes can be moved to speed up, slow down, or retime the traverse with zero effect on the path's shape; the look-target can be keyframed to hold, pan, or snap to a different point of interest with zero effect on either the path or the camera's speed along it.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Not applicable directly — an authoring-architecture benefit; its payoff is downstream flexibility (independently adjustable arcs, easing, and points of interest) rather than a viewer-facing effect in itself.
use_cases: any camera move whose SHAPE (a smooth arc around a subject), SPEED (how quickly it travels that arc, and whether that speed is constant or eased), and SUBJECT OF ATTENTION (what it looks at, and when that attention shifts) are all independent creative decisions that will likely be revised separately during iteration
non_use_cases: a simple, short, linear point-A-to-point-B camera move with no curve and no independent look-target need, where ordinary direct keyframing of position and rotation together is simpler and this three-way split is unnecessary overhead (the source's own opening "simple dolly" example uses direct position+rotation keyframes, not this rig, precisely because it is this simple)
interactions: linear_interpolation_for_continuous_multi_shot_camera_flow (this same video) — once position (progress-along-path) and aim (look-target) are decoupled into separate channels, BOTH must be given matching easing styles for the combined result to read correctly, per that entry

constraint_influence_crossfade_for_instantaneous_shot_cuts (this same video) — the natural next step once one path+target rig exists: a second path (and, optionally, a second target) can be swapped in via influence crossfade to change shots without touching this same camera object or its aim rig
cadence_representation: A clear architectural gap: Cadence's camera item has ONE `@origin` CFrame track, which fuses position and rotation into the SAME keys on the SAME timeline — there is no equivalent of a separately-keyframed look-target object, and no notion of a path-shape/progress-along-path split at all (Cadence has no curve/spline object type, and no constraint system analogous to Follow Path). Authoring this video's decoupled rig in Cadence today would require either baking the look-target's independently-keyed rotation into the SAME `@origin` track by hand at every frame the two need to diverge (losing the independence entirely), or treating the look-target as a separate rig part and computing the camera's aim toward it as a manual, one-off calculation rather than a maintained relationship — Cadence has no `Track To`-equivalent constraint that would keep a camera's rotation continuously pointed at another item's position automatically.
control_surface: `set_keyframe` on the camera's single `@origin` CFrame track is the only existing surface; no path/curve object type, no progress-along-path abstraction, and no look-at constraint exist to decompose it further.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js` can measure the fused `@origin` track's position and rotation over time, but cannot distinguish or separately report a "path shape" versus "progress along it" versus "aim," since Cadence's data model does not represent those as separate things in the first place.
generation_or_modification_methods: not applicable — no authoring surface exists for any of the three channels independently; `set_keyframe` only ever sets the one fused `@origin` value at a time.
failure_modes: (in Blender, the source's own named pitfall) adding a third raw position keyframe to bend a two-keyframe straight-line move into a curve, producing a harsh, cusped turn rather than a smooth arc — solved specifically by routing position through an authored curve object instead of more raw position keys

a curve object with too low a sampling resolution, producing a visibly jagged/faceted camera path even though the underlying shape is smooth — the source's own noted fix is raising the curve's resolution setting, independent of any keyframe timing
roblox_considerations: Roblox has no native Follow-Path/Track-To constraint equivalent either; reproducing this rig there would require a custom script sampling a `.PathInterpolate`-style curve (or Bezier/Catmull-Rom evaluation) and a manual `CFrame.lookAt`-equivalent toward a separately-tracked target position, recomputed every frame — the same three-way decoupling this video demonstrates, implemented by hand rather than via built-in constraints.
performance_implications: None beyond ordinary constraint evaluation cost in Blender; not evaluated for a Roblox-equivalent custom implementation.
examples: the source's own one-minute summary: "add a camera a curve object and an empty object add a follow path constraint to the camera... adjust the shape of the curve to alter the camera motion path and now animate the offset of the follow path constraint to make the camera move along the curve then add a track 2 constraint to the camera and use the empty target object... animate the position of the empty object to control where the camera is looking at" (video @ 01:16–01:48)

the harsh-turn failure mode demonstrated directly: "if I want to have a more curved motion... add another keyframe to have more like a curved shape you can see that this won't work it will get this very ugly movement for the camera with a harsh turn" (video @ 09:36–09:56), immediately preceding the curve-object solution
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/COwENnPwWJ8 @ 01:09–01:48, 09:36–14:35 — Zach Weinert (CG Boost) both summarizes and builds the full three-channel rig live, including the specific failure mode it solves; experimental until validated
